questions.stem: A 74-year-old man presented with fever and malaise. His past medical history included severe aortic stenosis and ascending aortic aneurysm, for which he received concomitant aortic valve replacement and aortic root repair 2 years previously. The patient had well-controlled diabetes but no other comorbidities. Physical exam revealed a new murmur. Investigations: Hemoglobin 8.2 g/dL HIV Ag/Ab negative Routine blood cultures ×3 pairs negative Mycobacterial blood culture positive after 2 weeks of incubation
questions.lead_in: What organism is most likely to be responsible?
questions.explanation: Mycobacterium chimaera This is a case of M. chimaera-related endocarditis following a valve replacement surgery. High level of suspicion is needed to make the diagnosis and to send the appropriate cultures. Incubation period for symptom presentation can be as long as 5 years. Slow rate of growth and absence of underlying immunodeficiency can help you eliminate the other options.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg IV q12h). (2) Daptomycin (8-10 mg/kg IV q24h). b) Add rifampin (900 mg IV q24h or 300 mg PO q8h) for the duration of therapy, together with gentamicin (3 mg/kg IV q24h) for the first 2 weeks. Rifampin is added specifically because it helps kill bacteria adherent to the foreign/prosthetic material and must never be used alone (selects resistance at ~10^-6).

cohort_answer.text: Vancomycin; Daptomycin. || Rifampin (x6 weeks) + gent (x2 weeks).

questions.model_answer: a) The HACEK group, the leading gram-negative cause of endocarditis: (1) Haemophilus (2) Aggregatibacter (3) Cardiobacterium (4) Eikenella (5) Kingella. (Healthcare-associated PVE also favours Pseudomonas, Serratia, Acinetobacter and Stenotrophomonas.) b) Triple-drug regimen for MRSA PVE: (1) Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h (trough 10-20 ug/mL) for >=6 weeks; (2) Rifampin 300 mg PO or IV q8h for >=6 weeks (start after ~2 days of effective therapy); (3) Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV/IM in 2-3 divided doses for the first 2 weeks.

questions.model_answer: a) Nontuberculous mycobacterial (NTM) prosthetic valve endocarditis, in particular Mycobacterium chimaera (a Mycobacterium avium complex member linked to contaminated heater-cooler units), which presents months to years after surgery (median 21 months) with an indolent, culture-negative picture. b) (1) Mycobacterial blood cultures; (2) tissue/valve sampling for mycobacterial culture plus broad-range PCR/16S sequencing (18F-FDG-PET/CT is a useful adjunct given negative echo). c) Prolonged multidrug antimycobacterial therapy with early surgical valve replacement: a macrolide-based MAC regimen (azithromycin + ethambutol + rifampin/rifabutin), adding amikacin for severe disease, continued for many months to lifelong suppression.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific azithromycin/ethambutol/rifampin MAC regimen for M. chimaera follows ATS/IDSA NTM guidance; the chapter gives only the general NTM-PVE principle (>=2 active drugs plus surgery).

cohort_answer.text: NTM: M. chimaera. Diagnostic tests: Mycobacterial blood cultures; tissue samples for culture, sequencing or PCR. Treatment: prolonged course of Azithromycin, Ethambutol, and Rifampin (same as cavitary MAC); severe disease may require aminoglycosides; surgery often suggested if possible

questions.model_answer: Triple-drug regimen: (1) Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h (trough 10-20 ug/mL) for >=6 weeks; plus (2) Rifampin 300 mg PO or IV q8h for >=6 weeks; plus (3) Gentamicin 3 mg/kg/day IV/IM in 2-3 divided doses for the first 2 weeks.

cohort_answer.text: Vancomycin IV (~30 mg/kg/d in 2 doses, target trough 10-20), minimum six weeks. Rifampin IV/PO 900 mg in 3 divided doses, minimum 6 weeks. Gentamicin IV/IM 3 mg/kg/d in 2-3 divided doses, 2 weeks. Gentamicin should be administered for the initial 2 weeks of therapy with either beta-lactam or vancomycin-containing regimens; if a strain is resistant to gentamicin, a fluoroquinolone may be used if the strain is susceptible.

questions.model_answer: a) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE), recommended in all suspected PVE: confirms the diagnosis (vegetation, Duke major criterion) and detects perivalvular complications (abscess, dehiscence, fistula) that would mandate surgery and define treatment duration. b) (1) Catalase-negative, gram-positive cocci in pairs/chains; (2) bile-esculin positive and grows in 6.5% NaCl (PYR positive). c) Production of aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (acetyl-/phospho-/nucleotidyl-transferases); acquired by horizontal gene transfer via plasmids/transposons. d) Because of high-level resistance to both aminoglycosides, use the double beta-lactam regimen: Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h plus Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h for a minimum of 6 weeks.
questions.beyond_mandell: Bench characteristics (catalase, bile-esculin, PYR, 6.5% NaCl) and the enzymatic mechanism/plasmid acquisition are standard microbiology, not detailed in this chapter.

questions.model_answer: a) TEE (with repeat blood cultures): confirms PVE and identifies perivalvular complications (abscess, dehiscence), thereby determining the need for surgery and the treatment duration. b) Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (acetyl-/phospho-/nucleotidyl-transferases) that alter the drug and prevent 30S ribosomal binding, abolishing cell-wall-agent synergy. c) Double beta-lactam: Ampicillin 2 g IV q4h plus Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h for a minimum of 6 weeks (high-level resistance to both aminoglycosides precludes a synergistic aminoglycoside). d) (1) Catalase negative; (2) Bile-esculin positive (and PYR positive).
questions.beyond_mandell: Enzymatic resistance mechanism and biochemical test results are standard microbiology, not explicitly in this chapter.

cohort_answer.text: Investigation: TEE or repeat blood cultures; if confirms IE, would change duration of treatment and likely need for surgery. Mechanism: Aminoglycoside modifying enzymes (acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases, or nucleotidyltransferases) altering the aminoglycoside and its ability to bind 30S ribosome subunit. Treatment: Ampicillin 2g IV q4h + Ceftriaxone 2g IV q12h x6 weeks. Biochemical tests: Catalase negative; Bile Esculin positive; PYR positive

questions.model_answer: For enterococci resistant to penicillin, aminoglycoside and vancomycin (VRE), only case-report-level options exist: (1) Linezolid 600 mg IV or PO q12h for >=6 weeks (monitor for myelosuppression/neuropathy); (2) Daptomycin 10-12 mg/kg IV q24h for >=6 weeks (often combined with ampicillin/beta-lactam for synergy). Surgical valve replacement with a prolonged (>=8 week) postoperative course should be considered when no effective bactericidal regimen exists.

questions.model_answer: a) Transesophageal echocardiography to confirm/exclude prosthetic-valve endocarditis, since prosthetic valve plus monomicrobial E. faecalis bacteremia is high risk and the finding dictates regimen and duration. b) Because HLR abolishes aminoglycoside synergy, use ampicillin plus ceftriaxone (2 g q4h + 2 g q12h) for 6 weeks (prosthetic-valve endocarditis). c) The most common mechanism is a bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme, AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2")-Ia, conferring high-level gentamicin resistance; it is acquired horizontally on mobile genetic elements (plasmids/transposons). d) (1) PYR (pyrrolidonyl arylamidase) positive; (2) bile-esculin hydrolysis positive (also growth in 6.5% NaCl, leucine aminopeptidase positive).

parts.text: What is the reason for testing aminoglycoside high-level resistance?
What is the mechanism of high-level resistance?

parts_raw.text: A) What is the reason for testing AG high level resistance?
B) What is the mechanism of high level resistance?
C) If streptomycin was used instead of gentamicin, what is the major disadvantage?

questions.model_answer: a) Endocarditis requires bactericidal therapy, but beta-lactams alone are not reliably bactericidal against enterococci; adding gentamicin or streptomycin produces synergistic killing (>=2 log10 increase at 24 h). HLR to both aminoglycosides abolishes this synergy, so testing determines whether an aminoglycoside can be added or whether ampicillin plus ceftriaxone must be used instead. b) A bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme, AAC(6')-Ie-APH(2")-Ia. c) Streptomycin mandates serum drug-level monitoring (narrow therapeutic window) and carries significant, often irreversible ototoxicity/vestibular toxicity; HLR to streptomycin arises by a separate mechanism (30S ribosomal mutation or streptomycin adenylyltransferase).

cohort_answer.text:
If high level AG resistance exists, we cannot use AG (except streptomycin) for synergistic treatment
Bifunctional aminoglycoside-modifying enzyme AAC(6')-IE-APH(2")-Ia
Need access to lab for rapid streptomycin level testing; Need CrCl >50; Lack of familiarity amongst clinicians for streptomycin use; Drug availability; High rate of ototoxicity which may not be reversible

questions.model_answer: a) Possible prosthetic valve endocarditis due to enterococcus (persistent/relapsing enterococcal bacteraemia in a prosthetic valve patient); a negative TTE does not exclude it, so TEE is required. b) Agree with ampicillin but it is inadequate as monotherapy - enterococci require synergistic combination therapy. As the strain has high-level resistance to both gentamicin and streptomycin, add Ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h (double beta-lactam) rather than an aminoglycoside, for a minimum of 6 weeks. c) No standard surgical indication is present at this point (TTE negative, no heart failure, valve dysfunction, perivalvular extension, emboli or uncontrolled infection). Relapsing/persistent infection despite adequate therapy for >5-7 days, or later demonstration of perivalvular complications, would be an indication.

cohort_answer.text:
Possible prosthetic valve IE
Agree but suggest adding Ceftriaxone 2g iV q12h for synergy. Min duration for prosthetic valve IE is 6 weeks
No surgical indications at this time (unless it was relapsing PVE). "Standard indications for surgery are severe heart failure, severe valve dysfunction, prosthetic valve infection, invasion beyond the valve leaflets, recurrent systemic embolization, large mobile vegetations, or persistent sepsis despite adequate antibiotic therapy for more than 5-7 days"
